clarifyingQuestions: Can either array be empty?
Can the arrays contain duplicates?
Is the tie rule applied to a first and then b?
hints: Because both arrays are sorted, moving the pointer at the smaller value is the only move that can shrink the gap.
Find the minimum difference first; tie-breaking is easier as a second pass.
For a fixed a the best partner is a - d before a + d; scan A in ascending order and stop at the first a with a partner.
invariants: both pointers only move forward
d never increases during the first pass
the first a found in the second pass is the smallest a with a partner at distance d
chooseWhen: Closest-pair queries over two sorted sequences
tradeoffs: Two passes keep the tie rule simple; a single pass with careful tie handling saves a constant factor

clarifyingQuestions: Do non-positive scores need any operations?
What makes the task impossible?
Must x be an integer?
hints: A score s > 0 needs exactly ceil(s / x) operations.
The total number of operations only falls as x grows, so the feasible x form a suffix.
Binary search between 1 and the maximum score; if even x = max needs more than k operations, return -1.
invariants: feasibility is monotone in x
x = max score needs exactly one operation per positive score
chooseWhen: Minimising a parameter under a monotone feasibility check
tradeoffs: Binary search costs a log factor; a closed form is not available because ceil sums are not invertible
hack2hire:686839500ed1b6fe83428ac8.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: smallest uniform decrement within an operation budget

clarifyingQuestions: Is the halved price rounded down, rounded, or kept fractional?
Must every voucher be used?
What is returned: the total cost or the per-item prices?
hints: The saving from halving p is p - floor(p / 2), which grows with p.
Each item's savings shrink as it is halved again, so taking the largest available saving each time is optimal.
Keep the current prices in a max-heap and halve the top vouchersCount times, stopping early when the top is 0.
invariants: each item's sequence of savings is non-increasing
the heap holds every item's current price
chooseWhen: Greedy allocation of a budget over items with diminishing returns
tradeoffs: A heap is simple; with very many vouchers, counting savings per threshold avoids per-voucher work
hack2hire:686833a90ed1b6fe83428ac3.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: halving vouchers, minimum total cost

Map each product to its department and count the distinct departments of the listed items.

clarifyingQuestions: Which x is returned when several minimise the distance?
Is nums sorted?
Can the total overflow 32-bit integers?
hints: The sum of absolute deviations is minimised at a median.
With an even count every point between the two middle values is optimal; the smaller middle value is the smallest optimal input value.
Sort a copy and take sorted[(n - 1) // 2], then sum the distances.

constraints: every row has length M and uses only "B" and "W"
clarifyingQuestions: Is the grid given as strings or as lists of characters?
Must rows and columns both be palindromes, or either?
Is the answer the count of flips or the resulting grid?
hints: Row symmetry ties (i, j) to (i, M-1-j); column symmetry ties (i, j) to (N-1-i, j).
Together they split the grid into orbits of at most four cells that must end up the same colour.
For each orbit, flip whichever colour is in the minority; middle rows and columns give orbits of size 2 or 1.
invariants: orbits partition the grid
each orbit contributes min(B, W) flips independently
chooseWhen: Symmetry constraints that group cells into independent classes
tradeoffs: Enumerating orbits directly avoids union-find but needs care with odd middle rows and columns
hack2hire:67a93084ea201244f8fae263.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: minimum flips to make all rows and columns palindromes

clarifyingQuestions: Is a flip a single character change, or a whole range?
Must exactly k flips be made, or at most k?
Is the answer the idleness or the flipped string?
hints: Check a candidate answer L instead of searching for flips directly: feasibility is monotone in L.
For L >= 2, flipping every (L + 1)-th character of a run of length r breaks it with floor(r / (L + 1)) flips and never merges runs.
L = 1 is special: the result must alternate, so compare against both alternating patterns.
invariants: the needed flip count is non-increasing in L
runs are counted on the original string
chooseWhen: Minimising a maximum with a monotone check
tradeoffs: The binary search adds a log factor; the per-run formula avoids simulating flips
hack2hire:699e789b6e73e4abccc9b2c8.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: shortest achievable longest run with at most k flips

clarifyingQuestions: Can a machine start a task at the instant another ends?
Are intervals given as [start, end] or [start, duration]?
Is the answer the count or an assignment of tasks to machines?
hints: The number of machines needed equals the largest number of tasks running at the same moment.
That maximum is reached at some task start.
Sort starts and ends separately and sweep, releasing ends at time t before taking starts at t.
invariants: running count = starts seen - ends seen
ends at t are processed before starts at t
tradeoffs: The two-array sweep avoids a heap but only gives the count, not an assignment
hack2hire:6a04d7ad3141bbc31efdd5c2.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: maximum overlap of half-open task intervals

constraints: level-order list with no trailing null
clarifyingQuestions: Return the path, the sum, or both?
Which path wins a tie?
How is the tree encoded?
hints: Every root-to-leaf path is found by a depth-first walk that carries the running sum.
Visiting the left child first makes the first strictly-better leaf the leftmost optimum.
Store parent links instead of copying paths, then walk back from the best leaf.
invariants: the carried sum equals the sum of the node's ancestors and itself
a later leaf replaces the best only when strictly smaller

tradeoffs: Iterative traversal avoids recursion limits on deep trees at the cost of explicit stacks

clarifyingQuestions: Can a task add energy (negative usage)?
Is the level checked only between tasks or also during a task?
Are there recharge stations or other rules after a task?
hints: The level after task i is b minus a prefix sum.
It stays positive exactly when b exceeds every prefix sum.
Track the largest prefix sum P; the answer is max(1, P + 1).
invariants: the running prefix sum is exact in integers
the answer is at least 1

tradeoffs: One pass is optimal; the result can reach about 1e14, which needs 64-bit or exact integers

Maintain counts in a hash map and the number of keys with positive count.
Shrink from the left while the window stays good, recording each length.

left never moves backwards

clarifyingQuestions: Are negative numbers allowed, and how is their parity defined?
Is a swap of any two indices allowed, or only adjacent ones?
hints: Only parities matter, and the final layout is fixed: E evens then the odds.
Every odd value in the first E slots must leave, and each swap can fix one of those together with one misplaced even.
Count the odd values among the first E positions.
invariants: misplaced odds in the prefix = misplaced evens in the suffix
one swap fixes at most one misplaced pair
chooseWhen: Counting the cost of a partition by swaps
tradeoffs: The count is exact for arbitrary swaps; adjacent swaps would need an inversion count instead

clarifyingQuestions: How is the N-ary tree given?
In which order should values within a day appear?
What is returned for an empty tree?
hints: A node is removed on the day after its last child is removed.
So the removal day of a node is its height plus one, with leaves at height 0.
Compute heights bottom-up in reverse breadth-first order and group values by height.
invariants: a node's height is one more than its tallest child
the root is alone on the last day
tradeoffs: Height grouping is linear; the day-by-day simulation is quadratic on chains

hints: With a single bracket type, a stack of "(" reduces to a counter.
A ")" with the counter at 0 has no partner.

constraints: n has no leading zeros and is at least 1
clarifyingQuestions: Strictly greater or greater-or-equal?
Can n have leading zeros?
How long can n be (does it fit in 64 bits)?
hints: A palindrome is fixed by its left half (with the middle digit).
Mirroring n's left half gives the smallest palindrome with that half; if it is not larger than n, the half must grow by one.
Incrementing an all-nines half carries out of the half: the answer is then 1, zeros, 1, one digit longer.
invariants: the output always has len(n) or len(n) + 1 digits
mirroring keeps the left half unchanged
chooseWhen: Big-number string manipulation without integer conversion
tradeoffs: String arithmetic handles any length; native integers only work up to 15 digits in JavaScript
hack2hire:67883eb4e20f8f324213c2a2.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: smallest palindrome strictly above a decimal string
